tool_summary: The Ruby interpreter. Can execute a visible inline expression (-e), an opaque script file, or drop into an interactive REPL (though irb is the more common REPL entry point).
platform_notes: Behavior of -e and bare invocation is consistent across MRI Ruby on Linux and macOS.

rules.description: The -e flag executes the given string as Ruby code. When that string is visible in the invocation, commandant can inspect it directly. This rule fires when the payload itself contains a known destructive pattern (system()/backticks shelling out to rm -rf, FileUtils.rm_rf, etc.), rather than merely flagging that Ruby was invoked.
rules.notes: Coarse string-sniff over the -e payload, not a recursive re-assessment. See R-INS-05.

rules.description: The -e flag executes the given string as Ruby code. The code is visible in the invocation and does not itself match a known destructive pattern, but any -e invocation still executes arbitrary Ruby including file I/O, network access, and shelling out.
rules.reversible_note: Reversibility depends on the executed code, which is visible in the -e argument and can be reviewed prior to execution, unlike a script file invocation.

rules.description: Invoking ruby with a script file path executes the file's contents, which are not visible in the command string itself and cannot currently be inspected by commandant. Treated as the worst case since the script's actions are entirely opaque.
rules.reversible_note: Reversibility depends entirely on the script's contents, which commandant does not inspect. Treated as the worst case. See R-INS-03.

rules.description: Bare invocation with no -e and no script argument reads from stdin as a script (or blocks waiting for input), rather than a fully interactive REPL like irb -- but is still an uncommon invocation in an autonomous agent context and worth flagging.
